days.learn: Dockerfiles: multi-stage builds, small images, non-root users
days.title: Multi-stage Dockerfile for the API
days.doneWhen: `docker build` produces an API image that runs as a non-root user, serves `/health` on port 8080 with all settings from environment variables, and a separate `migrator` build target produces an EF Core migrations bundle
days.brief:
### Why this matters
"Works on my machine" ends when the machine is an image. A multi-stage build compiles with the full SDK, then copies only the published output into a small runtime image: smaller downloads, fewer vulnerabilities, nothing to compile with if an attacker gets in. Running as a non-root user limits damage further. Writing a multi-stage Dockerfile from memory is this week's checkpoint.

### What you'll build
On a new branch `feature/ship-it`:
- `api/Dockerfile` with stages: `build` (from the .NET 10 SDK image), `publish`, `migrator`, and `final` (from the ASP.NET Core 10 runtime image)
- Layer caching: copy the `.csproj` files and restore first, then copy the source
- `dotnet publish -c Release` with no app host, into `/app`
- The final stage running as the non-root user the .NET images provide (`USER $APP_UID`), listening on 8080
- A writable uploads folder owned by that user (week 14's local storage, until tomorrow's swap)
- `api/.dockerignore` excluding `bin`, `obj`, tests output, `.git`, `.env` and user secrets
- A `migrator` stage that builds an EF Core migrations bundle (`dotnet ef migrations bundle`) into a single executable, used on Wednesday and Friday
- The `docker` ecosystem added to Dependabot (week 18) for the base images

### Step by step
1. Read the multi-stage page. Sketch the stages and what each copies.
2. Write the build and publish stages. Build once, then change one `.cs` file and build again: restore should come from cache.
3. Write the final stage. Only the published output is copied.
4. Set the user and port. Confirm with `docker run` and `docker exec <id> id` (or `whoami`).
5. Run the container with settings as environment variables (`Jwt__SigningKey`, `ConnectionStrings__JobHunt`) pointing at your local SQL Server.
6. Add the migrator target and build it with `--target migrator`.
7. Record the image size in the PR. Try a chiseled Ubuntu runtime variant and compare.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The runtime image contains no SDK and no source
- [ ] The container runs as a non-root user
- [ ] Changing code does not invalidate the restore layer
- [ ] No secret is baked into any layer
- [ ] Migrations are a separate artifact, not run at app start-up

### Hints
- `docker history <image>` shows each layer and its size; secrets copied in an early stage can still leak if copied forward.
- The .NET 8 and later images listen on port 8080 by default because non-root users cannot bind to port 80.
- The .NET SDK can also build images without a Dockerfile (container publishing). Knowing the Dockerfile way first makes that easy to read.

```dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY src/*/*.csproj ./  # TODO: keep the folder structure for restore
# TODO: restore, copy source, publish to /app
```

### Common mistakes
- `COPY . .` before restore, so every change re-downloads packages.
- `appsettings.Development.json` or `.env` copied into the image.
- Running migrations automatically on every app start with several instances racing.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add an image scan to your local routine and compare the default and chiseled variants.

### Check your understanding
- Why multi-stage?
- Why non-root, and why port 8080?
- Why are migrations a separate step?

days.learn: Serving a SPA from nginx; build-time vs run-time configuration
days.title: Dockerfile for the web app served by nginx with SPA fallback
days.doneWhen: The web image serves the SPA through nginx, a deep link such as `/applications/<id>/notes` reloads without 404, `/api`, `/hubs` (WebSocket) and a 5 MB upload work through nginx, and the CSP from week 18 arrives as a response header
days.brief:
### Why this matters
In development the Vite proxy made `/api`, `/hubs` and `/hangfire` same-origin. Production needs a real replacement. Serving the built SPA from nginx and proxying `/api` and `/hubs` to the API keeps everything on one origin: no CORS, and week 8's `SameSite=Strict` refresh cookie keeps working. Knowing build-time vs run-time configuration for a SPA is a classic deployment question.

### What you'll build
- `web/Dockerfile`: a Node LTS stage running `npm ci` and `npm run build`, then an unprivileged nginx stage serving `dist`
- `web/nginx.conf`:
  - `try_files $uri /index.html` for SPA routes
  - long cache with `immutable` for hashed `/assets/`, `no-cache` for `index.html`
  - `location /api/` and `location /hubs/` proxying to the API, with the WebSocket upgrade headers for `/hubs`
  - `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` set, so the API (week 18) sees the real client once nginx is a trusted proxy
  - `client_max_body_size` a little above week 14's 5 MB limit
  - the week 18 CSP and security headers with `add_header ... always`
- `/hangfire` not routed in production (Friday decides how admins reach it)
- `web/.dockerignore` excluding `node_modules`, `dist` and `.env*`

### Step by step
1. List what the Vite proxy did for you in weeks 3, 8, 14 and 15. Each line needs an nginx equivalent or a decision.
2. Write the Dockerfile. `npm ci` uses the lock file exactly.
3. Write the server block: static files and SPA fallback first, then the proxy locations.
4. Add the WebSocket headers for `/hubs`: HTTP/1.1, `Upgrade` and `Connection`.
5. Run the web and API containers on one Docker network and test deep links, login refresh, live updates and an upload.
6. Configure the API's trusted proxies for the Docker network (week 18).
7. Note build-time vs run-time config: `VITE_` values are baked into the bundle. Because every URL is relative, JobHunt needs no runtime config; write that down.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Deep links reload correctly
- [ ] Assets are cached long, `index.html` is not
- [ ] API, hub and uploads work through nginx
- [ ] The API sees the real client IP and scheme
- [ ] The CSP is a header, not a meta tag

### Hints
- `add_header` in a `location` replaces headers from the outer block; repeat them or use an include file.
- If you ever need runtime config, serve a small `config.json` generated when the container starts, instead of rebuilding per environment.
- An unprivileged nginx image listens on 8080, matching the API's non-root approach.

```nginx
location /hubs/ {
    proxy_pass http://api:8080;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    # TODO: Upgrade and Connection headers, forwarded headers
}
```

### Common mistakes
- Missing SPA fallback, so refreshing a deep link returns 404.
- Caching `index.html` for a year, so users never get new releases.
- Forgetting `client_max_body_size`, so uploads fail with 413 only in production.

### Stretch (optional)
- Enable gzip or Brotli for text assets and measure the difference.

### Check your understanding
- Why same-origin routing instead of CORS?
- What is baked in at build time, and how would you change config without rebuilding?
- Why cache assets and `index.html` differently?

days.learn: docker compose: services, health checks, volumes, networks
days.title: docker compose up runs API, web, SQL Server, Redis and RabbitMQ
days.doneWhen: From a fresh clone with only `.env` filled in, `docker compose up` starts SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, the SMTP catcher, Azurite, the migrator, the API and the web app in order, the app works at one URL, and uploaded files land in Blob storage

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: Use Azurite for local Azure Storage development

days.brief:
### Why this matters
JobHunt now needs seven services. Compose turns a page of setup instructions into one command, and it is how reviewers will run your portfolio project. Health checks and start order are where it gets real: an API that starts before SQL Server is ready crashes. Containers also have disposable disks, so files saved inside one vanish on redeploy; that is why storage moves to Blob today.

### What you'll build
- `compose.yaml` at the repo root with `sqlserver`, `redis`, `rabbitmq` (management image), `mailpit` (or your catcher), `azurite`, `migrator`, `api` and `web`
- Health checks: `sqlcmd` for SQL Server, `redis-cli ping`, `rabbitmq-diagnostics -q ping`
- `depends_on` with `service_healthy`, and the API waiting on the migrator with `service_completed_successfully`
- Named volumes for SQL data and RabbitMQ; only `web` (and dev tool UIs) publish ports
- Secrets from `.env` (week 18), never in `compose.yaml`
- `BlobFileStorage : IFileStorage` (week 14) in Infrastructure using `Azure.Storage.Blobs`, chosen by `FileStorage:Provider`; Azurite locally, a real account later
- `OrphanFileCleanupJob` (Hangfire, weekly): deletes blobs with no `Attachment` row that are older than a day, and attachment files of applications hard-deleted by the week 14 purge idea

### Step by step
1. Write the infrastructure services first and get each healthy with `docker compose ps`.
2. Add the migrator: it runs the bundle from Monday against SQL Server and exits.
3. Add the API and web with `build:` pointing at their Dockerfiles and settings via `environment` and `.env`.
4. Implement `BlobFileStorage`: upload with the generated key, open a read stream, delete if exists. Switch with configuration only.
5. Upload a file and find it in Azurite. The week 14 tests should pass with either provider.
6. Write the orphan cleanup job. The one day grace period protects uploads whose database row is still being saved.
7. Delete everything with `docker compose down -v` and start again from scratch.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One command starts the whole stack from nothing
- [ ] Services start in the right order without crash loops
- [ ] No secrets in `compose.yaml`
- [ ] File storage is swapped by configuration, with no code changes in Application
- [ ] Orphaned files are cleaned up safely

### Hints
- Inside the Compose network, services reach each other by service name (`sqlserver`, `redis`), not `localhost`.
- The week 14 abstraction pays off now: only Infrastructure and configuration change.
- `docker compose logs -f api` is your friend when start order is wrong.

```yaml
api:
  build: ./api
  depends_on:
    migrator: { condition: service_completed_successfully }
    redis: { condition: service_healthy }
  # TODO: environment from .env, no published port
```

### Common mistakes
- `depends_on` without conditions, which only orders start, not readiness.
- Publishing every port to the host.
- Cleaning up files with no grace period and deleting uploads in flight.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add the trace viewer and log viewer from week 16 under a `tools` profile.

### Check your understanding
- What does a health check change about start order?
- Why must files leave the container's disk?
- How does the orphan job avoid deleting a file that is being uploaded?

days.learn: GitHub Actions: jobs, caching, test reports, required checks
days.title: CI workflow: build and test both apps on every pull request
days.doneWhen: Every pull request runs a workflow that builds and tests the API (with Testcontainers), lints, type-checks and tests the web app, runs Playwright, uploads test and coverage reports, fails below the coverage thresholds, and is a required check before merging
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Every check you wrote in weeks 11 to 19 is only useful if it runs on every change. Continuous integration makes "main is always green" a rule enforced by a machine. Dependabot's pull requests (week 18) now get tested automatically. Interviewers ask what your pipeline runs, how long it takes and how you keep it fast.

### What you'll build
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` triggered on pull requests and pushes to main
- Job `api`: set up .NET 10, cache NuGet packages, `dotnet build`, `dotnet test` with coverage (Docker is available on Ubuntu runners, so Testcontainers works)
- Job `web`: set up Node with npm caching, `npm ci`, lint, `tsc --noEmit`, `vitest run --coverage`
- Job `e2e` needing the other two: start the stack (or the E2E setup from week 19), install Playwright browsers, run the tests, upload the HTML report and traces on failure
- Coverage thresholds: Vitest `coverage.thresholds` in its config, and a .NET threshold that fails the job when merged line coverage drops (coverlet's MSBuild integration supports one, or a small script reading the Cobertura summary)
- Test results and coverage as artifacts and a short summary in the job summary
- A ruleset on main requiring the three checks and a pull request
- A CI badge in the README

### Step by step
1. Read the Actions quickstart and the workflow syntax for jobs, steps, `needs` and caching.
2. Write the `web` job first; it is the fastest to get green.
3. Add the `api` job. Exclude migrations from coverage as in week 11.
4. Set thresholds a little below today's numbers, so they stop regressions without blocking you.
5. Add the `e2e` job with `CI=true` so Playwright uses retries and never reuses servers.
6. Upload artifacts with `if: always()` for reports and `if: failure()` for traces.
7. Open a pull request that breaks a test on purpose, watch it fail, fix it.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every PR runs all three jobs
- [ ] Caching makes the second run noticeably faster
- [ ] Coverage below the threshold fails the build
- [ ] Failed E2E runs upload traces
- [ ] Main cannot be merged into without green checks

### Hints
- Put independent jobs in parallel; only E2E needs the others.
- Pin actions to a major version at least; Dependabot keeps them current.
- Secrets are not needed for CI: tests use containers and generated keys.

```yaml
jobs:
  web:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults: { run: { working-directory: web } }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      # TODO: setup-node with npm cache, ci, lint, typecheck, test with coverage
```

### Common mistakes
- One giant job that runs everything in sequence.
- Thresholds set at 100% or at 0%.
- E2E tests that silently reuse a stale local server in CI.

### Stretch (optional)
- Build both Docker images in CI on every PR without pushing them.

### Check your understanding
- What runs on every PR, and how long does it take?
- Why do coverage thresholds sit slightly below the current number?
- What makes a check "required"?

days.learn: Deploying containers to the cloud; migrations on deploy; scaling statelessly
days.title: CD to Azure Container Apps (or App Service) with migrations applied safely
days.doneWhen: Merging to main builds and pushes both images, runs the migrations bundle, then rolls out new Container Apps revisions; the live URL works with two API replicas (login, live updates, stats cache eviction, dashboard cookie) and PR "Ship it" is merged

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: Azure Container Apps overview
Microsoft Learn: SignalR hosting and scaling

days.brief:
### Why this matters
Deploying is easy; deploying safely and at scale is the interview topic. Two instances expose every piece of in-memory state: caches, SignalR groups, encryption keys, files. Migrations must run once, before the new code, and stay compatible with the old code still running. This day closes many threads from earlier weeks.

### What you'll build
- `.github/workflows/cd.yml` on push to main: build and push images (GitHub Container Registry or Azure Container Registry), run the migrations bundle as a one-off step or Container Apps job, then update both apps
- Azure login with OpenID Connect federated credentials: no cloud secrets stored in GitHub
- Container Apps: `web` with external ingress, `api` with internal ingress behind nginx, a managed identity reading Key Vault (week 18) and Blob storage
- Stateless API checklist:
  - output cache: the Redis-backed output cache store (a separate ASP.NET Core package) so week 13's per-user tag eviction reaches every instance
  - SignalR: the Redis backplane, so week 15's group sends reach users connected to another instance
  - Data Protection keys persisted to Redis or Blob, so the week 14 dashboard cookie works on any instance
  - outbox publisher (week 17): row locks that skip locked rows, so two instances never publish the same batch
- Forwarded headers in production: trust the platform's ingress as the proxy and write down the trade-off
- Hangfire dashboard: off by default in production, or behind the admin cookie policy over HTTPS, never public

### Step by step
1. If you have no Azure subscription, use App Service or any container host, or write the workflow and run it against a staging resource group later. The decisions matter more than the provider.
2. Create the resources once (portal or CLI) and record them in `DEPLOY.md`.
3. Write the workflow: build, push, migrate, deploy. A failed migration stops the rollout.
4. Make migrations backwards compatible: expand first (add nullable columns), contract in a later release.
5. Work through the stateless checklist and set replicas to 2.
6. Test on the live URL: log in, open two tabs, move a card, check the stats update.
7. Run all builds and tests, push, open PR "Ship it", review and merge. Watch the first deploy.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Merging to main deploys without manual steps
- [ ] Migrations run once per release, before new code serves traffic
- [ ] No secrets stored in the repository or in GitHub for Azure access
- [ ] Two API replicas behave like one
- [ ] The Hangfire dashboard is not publicly reachable

### Hints
- Rate limits (week 13) are per instance in memory; note it, or move them to a distributed store if it matters.
- Hangfire with SQL Server storage already coordinates several servers.
- Health checks on `/health` let the platform restart unhealthy replicas.

```yaml
- name: Migrate database
  run: ./efbundle --connection "${{ steps.conn.outputs.value }}"
  # TODO: then update the api and web container apps
```

### Common mistakes
- Running migrations on app start-up from every replica.
- Dropping a column the old version still reads during rollout.
- Testing scale-out with one replica and calling it done.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add a staging environment with a manual approval before production.

### Check your understanding
- Which JobHunt state would break with two instances, and how did you fix each?
- Why expand and contract migrations?
- Why OIDC instead of a stored cloud password?

days.title: Explain why the API must be stateless to scale out, with JobHunt examples, and write a multi-stage Dockerfile from memory
days.brief:
### The drill
Explain why the API must be stateless to scale out, with JobHunt examples, and write a multi-stage Dockerfile from memory, in 25 minutes.

### Rules
- Part 1 (about 10 minutes): blank page, explain out loud with two API instances drawn behind a load balancer.
- Part 2 (about 15 minutes): new empty folder outside the JobHunt repo with `dotnet new web`, then a Dockerfile.
- The outline says from memory for the Dockerfile: keep docs closed for the first attempt and note every lookup.
- No AI assistants, and no copying from JobHunt.

### Must include
- Part 1: at least five pieces of JobHunt state and where each lives now: output cache, SignalR connections and groups, Data Protection keys, uploaded files, the outbox publisher, rate limit counters
- Part 1: what breaks if each stayed in memory or on local disk
- Part 1: why migrations do not run on start-up
- Part 2: an SDK build stage, restore before copying source, publish, a runtime stage, a non-root user and port 8080
- Part 2: a `.dockerignore`
- Part 2: build and run it, then call the endpoint

### Self-check
- [ ] Finished within 25 minutes
- [ ] Every state example had a fix
- [ ] The runtime image has no SDK
- [ ] A code change rebuilt without re-restoring packages
- [ ] You needed zero lookups, or you know exactly which ones to review

### If you got stuck
- Multi-stage API image: redo Monday.
- nginx and SPA serving: redo Tuesday.
- Compose and Blob storage: redo Wednesday.
- CI and coverage thresholds: redo Thursday.
- Deployment, migrations and statelessness: redo Friday.
